content: Diffuse brainstem glioma is a highly aggressive and devastating disease with a very poor prognosis. The most commonly employed treatment modality is conventional fractionated radiotherapy. However, there is currently no meta-analysis or systematic review available that evaluates the benefits or harms of radiotherapy in individuals with diffuse brainstem glioma. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of conventional fractionated radiotherapy, with or without chemotherapy, compared to other therapeutic approaches, including alternative radiotherapy techniques, in children and young adults aged 0 to 21 years with newly diagnosed diffuse brainstem gliomas. To identify relevant studies, a comprehensive search was conducted in databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE/PubMed, and EMBASE up to August 19, 2015. Additionally, conference proceedings from major oncology societies and trial registries were reviewed. No language restrictions were applied during the search. The inclusion criteria encompassed all randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-randomized trials (QRCTs), or controlled clinical trials (CCTs) that compared conventional fractionated radiotherapy (with or without chemotherapy) to other therapies, including different radiotherapy techniques, in the specified population. Two reviewers independently screened studies for inclusion, extracted data, assessed the risk of bias, and performed GRADE assessments. Disagreements were resolved through discussion. Analyses were conducted in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. Two RCTs met the inclusion criteria. The first trial, a multi-institutional study with 130 participants, compared hyperfractionated radiotherapy (a six-week course with twice-daily treatments of 117 cGy per fraction, totaling 7020 cGy) to conventional radiotherapy (a six-week course with once-daily treatments of 180 cGy per fraction, totaling 5400 cGy). The median overall survival (OS) was 8.5 months in the conventional group and 8.0 months in the hyperfractionated group. No significant differences were observed in OS (hazard ratio [HR] 1.07, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.75 to 1.53) or event-free survival (EFS) (HR 1.26, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.90) between the two groups. Radiological response (risk ratio [RR] 0.94, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.63) and toxicities were also similar. The quality of evidence was judged to be low for OS and EFS, and very low for radiological response and toxicities, indicating that further research is likely to impact the confidence in these estimates. The second RCT included 71 participants and compared hypofractionated radiotherapy (39 Gy in 13 fractions over 2.6 weeks, 3 Gy per fraction) to conventional radiotherapy (54 Gy in 30 fractions over six weeks, 1.8 Gy per fraction). The median OS was 7.8 months in the hypofractionated group and 9.5 months in the conventional group. Progression-free survival (PFS) was 6.3 months in the hypofractionated group and 7.3 months in the conventional group. No significant differences were observed in OS (HR 1.03, 95% CI 0.53 to 2.01) or PFS (HR 1.19, 95% CI 0.63 to 2.22) between the two groups. The most commonly reported adverse effects were local erythema and dry desquamation, particularly behind the auricles. Other toxicities were observed but did not differ significantly between the groups. The quality of evidence was rated as moderate for OS and low for PFS and toxicities. It is important to note that the small sample size of this trial may have limited its statistical power to detect clinically meaningful differences. Based on the currently available evidence, no definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding the role of radiotherapy in the management of newly diagnosed diffuse brainstem glioma in children and young adults. Further research is necessary, including adequately powered RCTs that consider all relevant outcomes. International multicenter collaboration is strongly encouraged. Given the potential benefits of hypofractionated radiotherapy in reducing treatment burden and improving the quality of life, this approach warrants further investigation.
